484.title: Let justice roll (Amos 5:21–24)
484.hook: God hates empty festivals; let justice roll down like waters
484.howItsDone: Christians and churches tie worship to service through food banks, advocacy and giving, and Amos 5:24 has been quoted in Christian movements for civil rights and economic justice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pentecost: Peter quoting Joel's promise of the spirit poured out on everyone. Your line: on all flesh.

Bethel was the king's own shrine in the northern kingdom of Israel, and its festivals were full: offerings, songs, the whole calendar kept. Then a man from the south, from the village of Tekoa, stood up there and spoke for God, and what he said would empty a room today: I can't stand this. Turn the music off. His name was Amos. By his own account he wasn't a prophet or a prophet's son, just a herdsman who gathered sycamore figs. And his line has ended up on protest signs.

In the King James Bible: "I hate, I despise your feast days, and I will not smell in your solemn assemblies." Then: "Take thou away from me the noise of thy songs." Noise. Their best hymns. Why? In the chapters around this one, Amos lists what's happening outside the shrine: the poor sold for a pair of shoes, bribes taken at the city gate, the rich lying on beds of ivory. The festivals went on as if none of it mattered. Then the line: "But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream." The Hebrew word behind judgment is mishpat, which can also be read as justice: things set right, especially for people who can't defend themselves. Some readers hear a picture underneath. That land has streams that roar in winter and are dry gullies by summer, and the Hebrew behind mighty can mean ever-flowing, a stream that doesn't fail. Not a flash flood of good intentions after a sermon: justice that doesn't dry up in August. Christians read this more than one way. Some hear that worship and justice belong together, not that worship is wrong. Others take it as a warning that God can't be pleased by ceremony that ignores the poor. Either way, the words travel. In 1963, Martin Luther King Jr. drew on this verse in his famous speech at the Lincoln Memorial, and Amos's river ran through the civil rights movement. A herdsman's sentence at a royal shrine, carried to the steps of a memorial.
screen: then, large: `LET JUDGMENT RUN DOWN AS WATERS.`

segments.voice: Let one unfair thing come to mind, one you can actually see: a coworker always talked over, a neighbor without a ride. Don't solve it in your head; ask what one small, real step could keep flowing after today, a call, a donation, a word spoken up. If you pray, bring that person or cause to God; if not, simply hold the step in mind.
Justice. Mishpat in Hebrew: things set right, especially for people who can't defend themselves, flowing like a stream that never runs dry.
Your line: justice like a river. Not a flash flood, but a stream that doesn't fail. Day four hundred eighty-four, done.

485.title: Jonah runs (Jonah 1)
485.hook: told to go east, Jonah takes a ship west, and sleeps through a storm
485.howItsDone: Christians read the book of Jonah as one short story, often in a single sitting; in Jewish practice the whole book is read in synagogue on the afternoon of Yom Kippur, and Christians in many churches hear it in Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Amos and mishpat: justice like a stream that doesn't fail. Your line: justice like a river.

The call comes, and it's the last thing Jonah wants. Go to Nineveh, that great city of Assyria, the empire Israel had most reason to fear, and tell them God has seen their wickedness. Nineveh is east, overland. So Jonah walks to the port of Joppa, finds a ship for Tarshish, somewhere far out at the western end of the known world, pays the fare, and climbs aboard. Not a no. Just the opposite direction, as far as a ticket can take him. The story runs four short chapters, and its hero is already running.

Read chapter one slowly and a word keeps coming back. Jonah went down to Joppa. He went down into the ship. When the storm hits, the King James Bible says: "Jonah was gone down into the sides of the ship; and he lay, and was fast asleep." Down, down, down. In Hebrew it's the same verb each time. Running from God, in this story, is a long slide downward. The ship is about to break apart. The sailors, who aren't Israelites, each cry out to their own gods and throw cargo overboard. And Jonah, the only prophet on board, sleeps in the hold until the captain wakes him and tells him to pray. When they cast lots and the lot falls on Jonah, he finally says who he is: "I am an Hebrew; and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, which hath made the sea and the dry land." He's running from the God who made the sea, by sea. He tells them to throw him overboard. And here's the detail that's easy to miss: they don't want to. They row hard for land first, trying to save him. Only when that fails do they cast him in, and the sea goes calm. The sailors end up in awe of God, offering sacrifices and making vows. In this chapter they come off kinder and more prayerful than the prophet. That's the story's sense of humor, and its point. Jonah isn't a hero yet. He's someone a lot of us recognize.
screen: `DOWN TO JOPPA, DOWN INTO THE SHIP.`
`RUNNING FROM THE GOD OF THE SEA, BY SEA.`
then, large: `HE LAY, AND WAS FAST ASLEEP.`

segments.voice: Let your mind go to the thing you keep buying a ticket away from: a conversation, a call you haven't returned, a decision, an apology. Don't scold yourself; just name the direction you're avoiding, east, and notice how much effort west is costing you. If you pray, tell God plainly where you've been running; if not, simply say it to yourself.
Jonah runs. Called east to Nineveh, he sails west for Tarshish, and goes down, down, down, until a storm stops him.
Your line: you can't outrun him. In this story, running only ever goes down. See you tomorrow.

486.title: Inside the fish (Jonah 2)
486.hook: three days in the dark, Jonah prays from the belly
486.howItsDone: Christians read Jonah 2 alongside Jesus's words about the sign of Jonah in Matthew 12, and some hear Jonah's three days in the fish as a picture of the resurrection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonah ran: a ticket west, a storm, and a prophet asleep in the hold. Your line: you can't outrun him.

The sailors let go, and the sea closes over his head. Seaweed. Cold. The last light going green, then gone. Then, in the King James Bible, a short, flat sentence: "Now the LORD had prepared a great fish to swallow up Jonah." Notice prepared. The fish isn't an accident, or a punishment out of nowhere. It was ready. And the story doesn't describe the inside of the fish at all. No ribs, no stomach, no smell. It skips straight to what Jonah does in there.

He prays. "Then Jonah prayed unto the LORD his God out of the fish's belly." Up to now, Jonah has done everything except pray. He slept while the sailors prayed; the captain had to shake him awake. Now, at the very bottom, three days and three nights in the dark, the words finally come. The prayer is shaped like a psalm, its lines echoing the Psalms, as if he reached for prayers he already knew. He describes drowning: waters closing in, weeds wrapped around his head, going down to the roots of the mountains. And: "out of the belly of hell cried I, and thou heardest my voice." Hell there is the King James word for Sheol, the place of the dead. He feels as far from God as a person can get. Yet the prayer ends in thanks, while he's still inside the fish, before anything has changed. Its last line is short: "Salvation is of the LORD." Then the fish spits him out onto dry land. One more thing: the book of Jonah never calls it a whale. The Hebrew says a great fish. The whale came later, in some translations of Jesus's words in Matthew, where he points to Jonah's three days in the dark as a sign of his own three days in the grave. Some Christians hear Jonah's prayer as Easter in miniature: someone given up for lost, praying from the bottom, and brought back up.
screen: `A PSALM FROM THE BOTTOM OF THE SEA.`
then, large: `SALVATION IS OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Jonah didn't wait to be out of the fish or tidy up first; he prayed from the dark, weeds around his head. So, wherever you are, on a bus, in bed, in a hard week, name plainly how things are right now, then find one thing to be grateful for before anything changes. If you pray, speak to God from exactly this spot; if not, say the honest words to yourself and let them be heard.
Great fish. What the book of Jonah actually calls the creature that swallowed him, prepared and ready, never once called a whale.
Your line: prayer from the belly. The thanks came before the rescue. That's day four hundred eighty-six.

487.title: Nineveh turns (Jonah 3)
487.hook: the enemy city repents, down to the cattle, and God relents
487.howItsDone: Some churches read Jonah 3 during Lent as a picture of repentance, and Jesus points to the people of Nineveh in Matthew 12:41 and Luke 11:32 as people who turned when they heard Jonah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great fish, and a prayer from the dark that ended in thanks. Your line: prayer from the belly.

Chapter three opens with a line almost funny in its patience. In the King James Bible: "And the word of the LORD came unto Jonah the second time." The second time. Same message, same city, as if the storm and the fish were a long detour. This time Jonah goes. Nineveh is huge, the story says, a city of three days' journey. Jonah walks one day in and delivers a sermon so short it barely counts. In Hebrew it's five words. In English: "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown." No call to repent. No promise of mercy. Just the warning.

"So the people of Nineveh believed God, and proclaimed a fast, and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them even to the least of them." The great city of the empire Israel feared turns, all of it, and fast. The king gets up off his throne, takes off his robe, puts on sackcloth and sits in the ash. His decree: no person and no animal is to eat or drink. Cattle and sheep too, covered in sackcloth, crying out. It's a little comic, cows in mourning clothes, but it's also complete: the whole city, down to the barn. The king's reasoning is humble: "Who can tell if God will turn and repent, and turn away from his fierce anger, that we perish not?" Who can tell. He doesn't presume. Then: "God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way." And God relented and did not destroy them. Jewish tradition calls this kind of turning teshuvah, coming back, and on Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, the book of Jonah is read aloud in synagogue. Christians in some churches hear it in Lent. And some readers hear a quiet twist in Jonah's five words: the Hebrew for overthrown can also mean turned over, changed. In forty days, Nineveh would be turned upside down. It was. Just not the way Jonah meant.
screen: then, large: `WHO CAN TELL IF GOD WILL TURN?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've quietly written off, your own private Nineveh; you don't have to like them, or trust them yet. Ask the king's question, who can tell, and imagine for a few breaths that they might turn. If you pray, pray for them by name; if not, leave the door to their changing open a crack.
Nineveh turns. The great enemy city hears five words and turns around, from the king to the cattle, and God relents.
Your line: even nineveh. Who can tell, as the king asked? Rest well; there's more Jonah tomorrow.

488.title: Jonah sulks (Jonah 4)
488.hook: angry at God's mercy, Jonah mourns a shady plant; God asks: shouldn't I pity Nineveh?
488.carry: mercy is wider than you like
488.howItsDone: Some Christians read Jonah 4 alongside Jesus's parable of the prodigal son, where the older brother also resents a welcome; sermons pair them to ask how people respond to mercy shown to others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nineveh turned, from the king down to the cattle. Your line: even nineveh.

If the book of Jonah were a movie, it would end after chapter three. The city repents, God relents, roll credits. But there's a fourth chapter, and it opens with the prophet furious. In the King James Bible: "But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was very angry." He's just watched a whole city turn at five words, and he's livid. Then he finally tells God why he ran. Not fear of the storm, or of the Assyrians. Something much more uncomfortable. He was afraid God would be kind.

His complaint sounds almost like a hymn: "I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness." Those words echo God's own self-description to Moses on the mountain in Exodus. Jonah knows the creed by heart. He just hates that it applies to Nineveh. So he asks to die, and God answers with a short, gentle question: "Doest thou well to be angry?" Jonah doesn't reply. He walks out east of the city, builds a little shelter, and sits to see what will become of it. Then the comic part. God makes a leafy plant grow up overnight to shade his head. The King James calls it a gourd; nobody is quite sure what plant the Hebrew means. And Jonah "was exceeding glad of the gourd." The one time the book calls him glad, it's over shade. Next morning God sends a worm, the plant withers, the sun beats down, a hot east wind blows, and Jonah wants to die again, this time over a plant. God makes his point: you pitied a plant you didn't plant or grow, which came up in a night and died in a night. Should I not pity Nineveh, that great city, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who can't tell their right hand from their left, and also much cattle? The book ends there, on a question. We never hear Jonah's answer; some readers hear that silence as an invitation. And the last words in English are much cattle. God's mercy, in this book, reaches even the cows.
screen: `GLAD OF A GOURD, THEN A WORM.`
then, large: `SHOULD NOT I SPARE NINEVEH?`

segments.voice: Think of a time someone got off easy and it bothered you, a coworker who wasn't fired, a sibling forgiven too fast, and let the irritation come up without judging it; Jonah felt it too. Then hear God's question, as gently as the story asks it: is it right for you to be angry? If you pray, bring it to God honestly, as Jonah did; if not, notice where it lives in your body.
Jonah sulks. Angry that God spared his enemies, glad of a shady plant, and left facing a question the book never lets him answer.
Your line: mercy is wider than you like. Even the cattle made it in. Day four hundred eighty-eight, done.

489.title: What does the Lord require? (Micah 6:8)
489.hook: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly with your God
489.howItsDone: Christians read Micah 6:8 in worship and sing it in hymns and songs, and Christian service and justice groups use it as a summary of faith in action.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonah sulked under a withered plant, and his book ended on God's question. Your line: mercy is wider than you like.

Micah chapter six is set in a courtroom. God has a case against the people and calls the mountains and hills as the jury. God lays out years of care: I brought you out of Egypt, I sent you Moses, Aaron and Miriam. Then a voice from the crowd answers, nervous, trying to settle. What do I bring? The offer starts climbing, like someone haggling against themselves. Calves? Thousands of rams? Ten thousand rivers of oil? My own firstborn child? An auction of guilt, every bid more extravagant than the last. Then the prophet cuts it off.

The answer, in the King James Bible: "He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?" He hath shewed thee. The answer isn't a secret; it has already been shown, and it was never more rams. Three things. Do justly: action, the same justice Amos wanted rolling like a river, fair dealing, especially for people with no power. Love mercy. The Hebrew word here is chesed: loyal, steady kindness, the love that keeps its promises. And Micah doesn't say do mercy. He says love it. Enjoy it. Want it. Then walk humbly with your God. Walk, not sit, not arrive: a whole life lived side by side, at God's pace. The Hebrew word for humbly turns up almost nowhere else, and some readers hear in it something quiet and careful, not putting on a show. One way to hold the three: each is a different part of a person, the hands, the heart, the feet. Jews have treasured this verse too. The Talmud records a teaching that the prophets kept summing up the Torah's many commandments into fewer and fewer, and Micah brought them down to three. Some Christians hear in it the same shape as Jesus's summary of the law: love God, love your neighbor. Short enough for a fridge magnet, big enough for a lifetime.
screen: `HE HATH SHEWED THEE: YOU KNOW IT.`
then, large: `WHAT DOTH THE LORD REQUIRE OF THEE?`

segments.voice: Say the three slowly in your head, justly, mercy, humbly, hands, heart, feet, and notice which one tugs at you: a fair thing you owe someone, a grudge you could set down, a need to perform or be right. Choose just one, and picture the moment today when you'll practice it: the room, the person, the hour. If you pray, offer that one choice to God; if not, just hold the picture steady.
Chesed. Hebrew for loyal, steadfast kindness: the mercy Micah says to love, beside doing justly and walking humbly with your God.
Your line: justly, mercy, humbly. The hands, the heart and the feet, all three. See you tomorrow.

490.title: Little Bethlehem (Micah 5:2)
490.hook: from the least of the clans shall come a ruler
490.howItsDone: Micah 5:2 is read in many churches during Advent and at Christmas services of lessons and carols, and it is quoted in Matthew 2 in the story of the wise men.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chesed, and Micah's answer to what the Lord requires: do justly, love mercy, walk humbly. Your line: justly, mercy, humbly.

Every country has towns like this. Not the capital, not the place on the postcards. A village you'd drive through on the way to somewhere else, where the gas station closes at six. Ancient Judah had one about six miles south of Jerusalem. Its one claim to fame was centuries old: a shepherd boy named David grew up there before he became king. Otherwise, a farming village on a hillside, with a homely name. Bethlehem is usually explained as house of bread. And Micah, the same prophet as yesterday, looked at it and said: watch this place.

In the King James Bible: "But thou, Bethlehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting." Ephratah was the old name of the clan and district around the village, telling it apart from another Bethlehem in the north. And look at little. Micah doesn't pretend Bethlehem is impressive; it's one of the least of Judah's clans. That's the point. Jerusalem in Micah's day was full of powerful people, and Micah has hard words for many of them. So the hope for a good ruler doesn't come from the palace. It comes from the hillside, from David's humble start. Jews have read this as a promise of a future king from David's family, and many still hold that hope. Christians read it as fulfilled in Jesus, born in Bethlehem. In Matthew's Gospel, when foreign wise men arrive asking where the king is to be born, Herod's scholars quote Micah. And Matthew's version has a lovely twist: where Micah says little, Matthew's quotation says "not the least." The birth changes the town's standing. This whole week has had that shape: Amos's river; Jonah running, praying, watching his enemies turn, sulking at mercy; Micah's three things; and now a little town. Over and over, God doesn't start where the power is.

segments.voice: Think of a small place that shaped you, a grandparent's kitchen, a back road, a classroom with a broken heater, or a small daily thing like the first cup of coffee. Picture it in detail, the smell, the light, the people, and let it be important for a minute, the way Micah let Bethlehem be important. If you pray, give thanks for that place and its people; if not, simply hold it with gratitude.
Little Bethlehem. A small farming village, David's hometown, where Micah said a ruler would come from, and where the Gospels say Jesus was born.
Your line: the least of the towns. Little, and then not the least. Day four hundred ninety, and another week on the path.
